sections.heading: Cedar Shake Roofing We Provide in Newark, NJ

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing provides 4 cedar shake roofing services across Essex County: new cedar shake installation, cedar shake repair and shake replacement, the ventilated interlayment deck system, and preservative and cleaning maintenance — for residential and select commercial properties.

runs.v: Cedar shake roofs are typically installed on spaced sheathing, or on solid plywood with a ventilating layer, so the assembly sheds water at the surface while the underside dries between rain events.

Cedar shake roofing lasts 20 to 40 years, per the Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau, against the single "Wood" service life of 25 years on the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart, because moisture management, not the cedar itself, sets the lifespan. With proper maintenance, cedar shake roofs can last 30 to 50 years; without maintenance, cedar shake roofs last only 15 to 20 years. A cedar shake roof needs at least 1.5 inches of air space beneath the shakes for drying, and north-facing and shaded slopes degrade faster, per Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau and NRCA guidance, so a Newark Quality Roofing cedar shake installation builds the ventilation path before the first course, because cedar shakes require proper ventilation to prevent rot.

sections.heading: Signs You Need Cedar Shake Roofing

c.v: Cupped, curled, and split cedar shakes across the roof

items.v: indicate advanced moisture-cycling degradation, the dominant cedar failure mode, and full replacement favors a roof with cupping or splitting across more than 25 to 30% of the shakes, per Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau and industry guidance.

c.v: A shake that cracks under light bending

items.v: fails the flex test, the InterNACHI indicator of advanced cedar degradation regardless of the surface appearance, per the InterNACHI roof inspection guidance.

c.v: Deep moss, lichen, and mildew growth prying the shake edges apart

items.v: retains moisture against the wood and accelerates rot, the moisture-driven decay that causes most premature cedar shake failure, per Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau guidance.

c.v: A cedar shake roof at or past its 20-to-40-year service life

items.v: signals replacement, because the Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau rates cedar shake at 20 to 40 years and the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart lists wood roofing at 25 years.

c.v: Deck or sheathing decay beneath cupped shakes across more than 15% of the roof area

items.v: crosses the structural threshold that favors replacement over selective shake repair, per industry repair-versus-replace guidance, because soft sheathing is structural damage that new shakes laid on top cannot fix.

c.v: Brown or yellow ceiling and wall stains

items.v: that spread after rainfall indicate an active roof leak or trapped attic moisture beneath the cedar field, per GAF and This Old House inspection guidance. Wet insulation in the attic means the leak has been running long enough to call for roof leak repair at the source, not a surface patch.

c.v: Clogged gutters and debris packed into valleys and keyways

items.v: hold standing water against the cedar after every storm, the condition that starts rot at the butts of the shakes and sends leaks into the walls below.

sections.heading: How Our Roofing Contractors Perform Cedar Shake Roofing

runs.v: Ventilated Deck and Interlayment System

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing contractors build the ventilation path first, setting the deck and interlayment so at least 1.5 inches of air space sits beneath the cedar shakes for underside drying.

runs.v: Trapped moisture causes most premature cedar shake decay, and north-facing and shaded slopes degrade faster, per Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau and NRCA guidance, so a Newark Quality Roofing cedar shake assembly spaces the deck and lays a breathable interlayment between courses to dry the underside between rain events. The NRCA and ARMA size attic ventilation at 1 square foot of net-free vent area per 150 square feet of attic floor, and balanced ventilation extends roof service life by up to 25%, per the NRCA. A vented attic also keeps the insulation dry through cold winters and sheds summer heat, which helps energy efficiency under a sun-loaded roof.
Hand-Graded Cedar Installation to CSSB Standards

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing hand-grades and installs each cedar shake with stainless-steel fasteners and corrosion-resistant flashing that match the 20-to-40-year cedar service life.

runs.v: Hand-split western red cedar varies in thickness and grain within a single graded bundle, so a Newark Quality Roofing installer sorts the thicker shakes to the eave courses and fastens with stainless-steel nails set to accommodate the wood movement that Essex County humidity and the average January low near 25.5°F drive, per NOAA 1991–2020 normals at Newark Liberty (EWR). Newark Quality Roofing sources cedar shakes graded to Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau standards. The exposed face of each course, the exposure, is set to the shake length, and a flashing inspection at chimneys, skylights, and walls comes before the new courses go on, because flashing transitions are a common leak source on any roof type.

sections.heading: Cedar Shake Grades and Thickness: What a Quote Should Name

c.v: Cedar shakes are graded under Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau rules, and the grade on the bundle label is the first line to check on any cedar quote, because grade decides how the wood holds up to Newark's humidity.

runs.v: Edge-grain wood resists cupping, heartwood carries the decay-resistant extractives, and clear wood has no knots to split around, so the top grades combine all three.

c.v: Premium grade

items.v: — Premium-grade shakes are 100% clear, 100% heartwood, and 100% edge grain, the most dimensionally stable cedar for a humid climate.

c.v: No. 1 grade

items.v: — No. 1 shakes are clear heartwood with a limited share of flat grain allowed, the usual grade for a long-life house roof.

c.v: No. 2 and lower grades

items.v: — Lower grades allow more flat grain and defects such as sapwood or knots; they cost less but cup, split, and decay sooner, and suit outbuildings better than a house.

c.v: Blue Label cedar shingles

items.v: — For sawn cedar shingles, the No. 1 Blue Label grade is the premium, all-heartwood, edge-grain product, with Red Label and Black Label as the lower grades.

runs.v: Thickness is the second decision. Handsplit and resawn shakes come in medium and heavy butt thicknesses, and a heavy shake carries more wood to weather away, so it outlasts a medium shake of the same grade. Most shakes come in 18- and 24-inch lengths, and the longer shake allows a larger exposure per course. Tapersawn shakes are sawn on both faces for a tailored, classic look, while straight-split shakes are split on both faces for the most rustic texture. The building code limits wood shakes to roof slopes of 4:12 or steeper, which is why low slope roofs never take cedar shakes. A proper repair matches the replacement shake to the existing grade, thickness, and exposure so the new pieces weather in with the old.

sections.heading: Cedar Shake Treatment, Maintenance, and Lifespan in Newark's Climate

c.v: Newark's climate works a cedar roof from both ends of the calendar: hot summers bake the exposed surface with UV, cold winters bring an average January low near 25.5°F, and the humid spring and fall keep the wood wet long enough for moss, algae, and fungi to take hold.

runs.v: That is why cedar shake roofs require maintenance more often than asphalt roofs due to environmental conditions, and why the same cedar roof can last 30 to 50 years properly maintained or only 15 to 20 years neglected. Maintained cedar can withstand harsh weather for decades, and roofing guides commonly cite a wind rating of up to 110 to 120 mph for a properly installed cedar shake roof, so in Essex County the bigger threat is not the high winds of a nor'easter but the moisture left behind afterward. Cedar shake roofing requires regular maintenance to prevent decay; the work is simple, but it has to happen on schedule.

c.v: Cedar treatment comes in two kinds: factory pressure treatment and field-applied maintenance coats.

runs.v: Pressure-impregnated fire-retardant cedar shakes carry a Class B or Class C rating under the Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau Certi-Guard program, and fire-retardant treated shakes meet local fire safety codes in residential areas, while pressure preservative treatment adds decay resistance beyond cedar's natural extractives. Field treatments are penetrating preservatives, often oil-based, with a fungicide and UV inhibitors, reapplied every 3 to 5 years for longevity; paint and film-forming sealers trap moisture in the wood and do not belong on a cedar roof. Zinc or copper strips near the ridge release metal ions with each rain that slow moss and algae growth down the slope. New cedar starts out a warm honey-brown and weathers to silver-gray within a year or two; a tinted preservative slows the color change, but no treatment stops it entirely.

c.v: Spring and fall

items.v: — Inspect the roof, the flashing at chimneys, skylights, and walls, and the attic below, because regular inspections of cedar roofs catch potential issues while they are still single-shake repairs.

c.v: Every year

items.v: — Clean the roof surface and the gutters. Cedar shake roofs need annual cleaning to prevent moss growth, and debris should be regularly removed from valleys and keyways, because packed leaves and needles hold standing water against the wood. A soft brush or low-pressure rinse does the job; high-pressure washing tears the wood fibers.

c.v: Every 3 to 5 years

items.v: — Reapply preservative treatment after cleaning, once the shakes are fully dry.

c.v: As needed

items.v: — Trim trees back to reduce debris and shade on cedar roofs, and promptly replace damaged cedar shakes to prevent water infiltration.

runs.v: Annual maintenance for cedar roofs averages $500 to $1,000, and over 40 years, maintenance costs add $25,000 to $50,000 to a cedar roof, the honest number to set against its natural beauty and service life. Between visits, check the roof from the ground with binoculars rather than walking on it; wet cedar is slippery, and shakes crack underfoot.

sections.heading: Commercial Cedar Shake Roofing We Provide

c.v: Newark Quality Roofing installs cedar shake roofing on commercial sloped roofs across Essex County, applying fire-treated cedar shakes graded to Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau standards where occupancy fire ratings apply.

runs.v: Untreated cedar shakes are nonclassified for fire under UL 790 and ASTM E108, while pressure-impregnated fire-retardant cedar shakes carry a Class B or Class C rating, and a Class A wood roof is reached only as a component assembly of Class B fire-retardant shakes over a fire-retardant cap sheet, per the Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau Certi-Guard program and the NJ Uniform Construction Code.

On a commercial building, repairing more than 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period requires a permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code, and a cedar-shake covering triggers complete removal rather than a recover-over under N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4. A Newark Quality Roofing commercial cedar maintenance schedule clears moss and debris and reapplies preservative on the Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau drying-driven cadence, because moisture against the wood causes most cedar shake decay.

Cedar belongs on the sloped parts of a commercial building — mansards, towers, entry roofs, and steep main roofs — because the 4:12 minimum slope for wood shakes rules out the flat sections, which take a membrane instead. Where cedar meets a membrane, the transition is flashed as its own detail, and that joint belongs on every maintenance visit.

sections.heading: Is a Cedar Shake Roof More Expensive Than Asphalt?

c.v: Yes: cedar shake roofs are more expensive upfront than asphalt shingles, and they cost more to keep.

runs.v: Architectural asphalt runs a typical NJ $6.50 to $11.00 per square foot, so a 2,000-square-foot roof costs about $13,000 to $22,000 in asphalt against roughly $24,000 to $50,000 in cedar, and cedar shake roofs require more maintenance than asphalt shingles every year after that. What the extra money buys is specific. Cedar shakes provide double the insulation of asphalt shingles, which improves energy efficiency and trims cooling costs under a sun-loaded roof, and cedar gives a house a natural beauty and a rustic, classic look that asphalt only imitates. Cedar shakes are also biodegradable and sourced from renewable timber. Over a 40-year span, architectural asphalt, which typically lasts 20 to 30 years in Newark's climate, will usually need one replacement while a maintained cedar roof may still be on the house, so the lifetime gap narrows, though it rarely closes once the $25,000 to $50,000 of cedar upkeep is counted.

c.v: Cedar shake roofing options include natural wood shakes and synthetic alternatives.

runs.v: Synthetic shakes offer lower maintenance than real cedar shakes, and composite cedar shakes resist moisture decay and have improved fire ratings, which makes them a common compromise where upkeep or fire risk rules out real wood. Real cedar remains the right choice where authenticity matters — a historic district, a house already roofed in cedar, or an owner who wants cedar's natural aesthetics and robust durability and will keep up the maintenance. Asphalt and other materials make more sense for an owner who will not clean and treat the roof on schedule, because an unmaintained cedar roof can fail in about half the life a maintained one reaches.

faqs.q: How long does a cedar shake roof last in New Jersey?

runs.v: A cedar shake roof lasts 20 to 40 years, per the Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau, against the single "Wood" service life of 25 years on the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart. With proper maintenance, cedar shake roofs can last 30 to 50 years, and without it they often last only 15 to 20 years, because moisture management, starting with at least 1.5 inches of underside air space, sets the lifespan.

faqs.q: What is the difference between cedar shakes and regular wood shakes?

runs.v: Cedar shakes are hand-split western red cedar, the wood species whose natural extractives resist decay, while general wood shakes include other species with less natural decay resistance. Cedar shake lasts 20 to 40 years per Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau standards.

faqs.q: How much does cedar shake roofing cost in Essex County, NJ?

runs.v: Premium cedar shake roofing in New Jersey runs $10 to $20 or more per square foot installed, and cedar shake repair runs $400 to $1,800. Maintenance runs about $0.15 to $0.60 per square foot every few years, and New Jersey pricing sits 10 to 40% above national figures because of higher labor costs and stricter code.

faqs.q: Do you need a permit for a cedar shake roof in Newark, NJ?

runs.v: Cedar shake re-roofing on a detached one- or two-family home counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and needs no construction permit. Commercial roofs above the 25% threshold and structural changes do require permits, and the code requires complete removal of an existing wood-shake covering rather than a recover-over.

faqs.q: Can individual cedar shakes be repaired without replacing the whole roof?

runs.v: Yes. Individual shake replacement works while cupping and splitting stay under 25 to 30% of the shakes and the deck stays sound; above that threshold, or with extensive deck decay, full replacement is the better value.

faqs.q: How do you maintain a cedar shake roof in the New Jersey climate?

runs.v: Clear moss and debris every year, reapply preservative every 3 to 5 years at roughly $0.15 to $0.60 per square foot, trim back overhanging trees, and replace damaged shakes promptly. The NRCA recommends roof inspections twice a year, in spring and fall, plus checks after major storms.

faqs.q: How do you prevent moss on a cedar shake roof in NJ?

runs.v: Keep the roof dry and clean: trim back overhanging branches so sun and air reach the shakes, clear leaves and needles from valleys, keyways, and gutters every year, and reapply a preservative with a fungicide every 3 to 5 years. Zinc or copper strips near the ridge add ongoing protection, and existing moss should come off with a soft brush or low-pressure rinse, never a high-pressure washer.

faqs.q: Does a cedar shake roof meet New Jersey fire code?

runs.v: Pressure-impregnated fire-retardant cedar shakes carry a Class B or Class C fire rating, while untreated shakes are nonclassified under UL 790 and ASTM E108. A Class A rating requires fire-retardant shakes over a fire-retardant cap sheet, per the Cedar Shake and Shingle Bureau Certi-Guard program.

faqs.q: What is the typical cost of installing a cedar shake roof?

runs.v: Industry guides put a cedar shake roof at about $12 to $25 per square foot installed, or $24,000 to $50,000 for a typical 2,000-square-foot roof, and New Jersey installs run $10 to $20 or more per square foot. Grade, thickness, pitch, tear-off, and treatment set where a given roof lands.

faqs.q: What is the 25% rule for roofing?

runs.v: The 25% rule refers to building-code limits on how much of a roof can be repaired in a 12-month period before the work is treated like a re-roof. In New Jersey, repairing more than 25% of a commercial building's roof area in 12 months requires a permit under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7, while roof covering work on a detached one- or two-family home is ordinary maintenance. Cedar roofers also use a separate rule of thumb: cupping or splitting across 25 to 30% of the shakes is the point where replacement beats repair.

faqs.q: Can you replace a cedar shake roof with asphalt shingles?

runs.v: Yes, after a full tear-off: New Jersey's code bars a recover over an existing wood-shake covering, and because cedar shakes are often laid over spaced sheathing, asphalt shingles need new solid plywood or OSB sheathing first. Check for historic district review before switching, since a change of roofing material on a designated property can require approval.

faqs.q: How do you repair a leaking cedar shake roof?

runs.v: Roof leak repair on cedar starts at the flashing around chimneys, skylights, valleys, and walls, then moves to the shakes above the stain. A cracked or cupped shake is split out, its old nails are cut, and a matched replacement is slid into place and fastened, so one shake can be replaced without disturbing the courses around it.
